   163	\section{What the cited soundness theorem requires: the import obligations}
   164	\label{sec:import-obligations}
   165	
   166	The quantum soundness theorem for the classical game inherits the constraint
   167	$m' \mid q$ solely because it is stated for the game just described; its
   168	proof fixes an admissible $q$ with $m' \mid q$, asserts that the game with
   169	simultaneity parameter $1$ is \emph{identical} to the two-prover tensor-code
   170	test for the Reed--Solomon tensor code $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$ of the same
   171	authors' \emph{Quantum soundness of testing tensor codes} (arXiv:2111.08131)
   172	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, and concludes by Theorem~4.7 there, instantiated with
   173	that theorem's auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ in that source,
   174	and written $K$ here to avoid clashing with the field exponent and the
   175	simultaneity parameter --- chosen as $(m')^3 d$.  Neither
   176	the asserted identity nor the instantiation is complete as stated, so the
   177	import carries two verification obligations, which this section details and
   178	which the blueprint's proof node for the soundness statement records as
   179	open.  Both obligations are independent of the divisibility question: they
   180	arise at every dimension, for the $\chi$-based game where it is defined and
   181	equally for the directly indexed variant proposed under the candidate
   182	repairs.
   183	
   184	\paragraph{The cited test.}
   185	In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
   186	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
   187	measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
   188	three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
   189	subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
   190	test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
   191	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
   192	direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
   193	send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
   194	$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
   195	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
   196	last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
   197	in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
   198	one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
   199	the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
   200	test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
   201	pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
   202	answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
   203	test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
   204	$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
   205	--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
   206	distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
   207	$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
   208	consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
   209	lines measurements, and with each other, up to
   210	$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
   211	\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.
   212	
   213	\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
   214	The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
   215	is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
   216	(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
   217	two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
   218	--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
   219	question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
   220	polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
   221	diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
   222	and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
   223	both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
   224	description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of
   225	the pair $(u,v)$, so the constructed measurement must average over the
   226	compatible indices and seeds; and the game's diagonal lines fix the
   227	\emph{first} $i-1$ coordinates where the test's subcubes fix the
   228	\emph{last} $j-1$, so the coordinate conventions must be aligned.  The
   229	construction must preserve projectivity and must match the law of the
   230	hidden-subcube pair with the law induced by the game's diagonal sampling.
   231	(ii)~The game's line questions carry the seed $s \in \F_q$; the test's
   232	carry only the line.  A strategy may depend on the seed beyond its class
   233	$\chi^{-1}(i)$, and removing this dependence runs into the fiber-averaging
   234	difficulty made explicit under the candidate repairs: averaging preserves
   235	the line-versus-point branches exactly but not the synchronicity branches.
   236	(iii)~The branch weights differ: each nontrivial cross-test has mass $1/3$
   237	in the test against $2/9$ in the game.  Once the per-branch predicates are
   238	matched, the intended bookkeeping bound is that the constructed strategy's
   239	rejection probability in the test is at most $\tfrac32$ times the game's
   240	rejection probability, up to the $O(1/(m'q))$ of item~(iv); this bound is
   241	the target of the obligation, not an established fact.
   242	(iv)~The game's predicate fixes an acceptance convention on diagonal
   243	questions with zero direction --- an event of probability at most
   244	$2/(m'q)$, recorded in the blueprint's remark on zero directions --- for
   245	which the test has no counterpart branch.
   246	Finally, the displayed conclusions of Theorem~4.7 pair one prover's points
   247	measurements with the other prover's tensor-codeword measurement, and the
   248	first prover's tensor-codeword measurement with the second prover's lines
   249	measurements, while the game-level statement asserts the point consistency
   250	in both directions; deriving the stated form uses the role symmetrization
   251	of the test and belongs to the correspondence.  None of these steps is
   252	difficult to state, but none is carried out in the source, and together
   253	they replace the asserted one-line identity by a reduction carrying its
   254	own value bound.
   255	
   256	\paragraph{Obligation 2: the parameter bound.}
   257	Theorem~4.7 requires $K \ge 12 m' t = 12 m' (d+1)$.  The source
   258	instantiates $K = (m')^3 d$, which meets the bound iff
   259	$(m')^2 d \ge 12(d+1)$: this holds for all $d \ge 1$ when $m' \ge 5$,
   260	holds at $m' = 4$ exactly when $d \ge 3$, and fails for every $d$ when
   261	$m' \le 3$.  In the game's parameter domain the dimension divides the
   262	admissible field size and is therefore a power of two, so the source's
   263	instantiation violates the hypothesis exactly at $m' \in \{1,2\}$ for
   264	every $d$ and at $m' = 4$ for $d \in \{1,2\}$ --- in particular, in the
   265	multilinear regime $d = 1$, at every dimension $m' \le 4$.  A candidate
   266	repair is to instantiate $K = \max((m')^3 d,\, 12 m'(d+1))$; the open
   267	obligation is then to re-absorb the error, that is, to check that
   268	$\mathrm{poly}(m',t,K)$ and $e^{-K/(m')^2}$ still collapse to the form
   269	$a(dm')^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bm'd})$ in the small-$m'$ cases where the
   270	maximum is $12m'(d+1)$ --- plausible, since there
   271	$e^{-K/(m')^2} = e^{-12(d+1)/m'}$ decays in $d$ at a rate comparable to
   272	$2^{-m'd}$ for $m' \le 4$, but not checked here.
   273	
   274	In the correspondence of Obligation~1, the only role of the divisibility

   276	mathematics does not need the divisibility.  The low

# Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

    15	The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

     8	/-!
     9	# The directly indexed low-degree game
    10	
    11	The low-degree game used by the Pauli-basis combining argument is needed in
    12	dimension `2 * m + 2`.  The existing conditionally linear game represents a
    13	coordinate index by an equally sized fiber in the scalar field and therefore
    14	requires the dimension to divide the field size.  This file gives the separate
    15	directly indexed variant which samples that index directly.
    16	
    17	The geometric line carrier records the sampled coordinate, and line evaluation
    18	uses an `Option` outcome rather than assigning a value when a point does not
    19	determine one.  The game retains the point, axis-line, and diagonal-line answer
    20	formats and the nine ordered type branches of the original low-degree game.
    21	
    22	The `Transport` modules relate the direct game to the seed-indexed game and to
    23	the low individual degree test: `Transport.Correspondence`
    24	identifies coordinates, answers, and the question law of the two QPBT
    25	presentations; `Transport.SeedFiber` dilates a seed-indexed strategy to a
    26	direct strategy by a correlated residue register, and `Transport.SeedFiberValue`
    27	shows that the dilation preserves the value exactly; `Transport.Questions`
    28	reads LDT lines as canonical direct questions and rebases direct answers;
    29	`Transport.Strategy` reads one coordinate of a projective direct strategy as a
    30	LDT projective strategy, with exact Born-weight formulas for both constructions;
    31	`Transport.Consistency` reexpresses the three single-polynomial LDT consistency
    32	relations in direct coordinates, the first two at a fixed tuple coordinate; and
    33	`Transport.BranchComparison`, `Transport.DiagonalRecursion`, and
    34	`Transport.PassConversion` convert a value bound of the direct game into the
    35	pass hypothesis of the low individual degree theorem for every
    36	coordinate strategy.  `GameValue` supplies the rejection calculus relating the
    37	direct value to the LDT branch weights.
    38	
    39	## References
    40	
    41	The underlying game is `def:ld-game` in
    42	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, with source origin
    43	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|

| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |

An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.

File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.

### Shared helpers

When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

## Review Checklist

Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.

- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
      implementation-phase labels)?
- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
      source does not use them that way?
- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
      that order of preference?
- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
      construction they support?
- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.

Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
relevant audit before changing names or prose.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:161:	The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.

The result of~\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} that underlies it is proved here as Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}: for every projective strategy passing the $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test of Definition~\ref{def:low-individual-degree-test} with probability at least $1-\eps$, that theorem produces measurements in $\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ satisfying consistency relations of the same shape as the three approximations of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}. Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} is not a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal} alone: a derivation from it would require, in addition, an equivalence between the typed game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}_{(q,m,d,1)}$ and the $(m,q,d)$ test of Chapter~\ref{chap:test} --- matching the two question distributions, the two win conditions, and the two error functions --- together with the extension from $k = 1$ to general $k$ by the reduction of~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP} cited above. Neither implication is proved in this chapter, and the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} given above does not invoke Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:482:The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} is the adaptation, to low individual degree, of the analysis of the quantum low-degree test of Natarajan and Vidick; it is developed in Chapters~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables} and~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} and concluded in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction}, where the argument is complete only modulo the unresolved divisibility obligation documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}. blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:517:	The paper writes the soundness function of the Pauli basis test with two different argument orders: $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps, m, d, q)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} and Lemma~\ref{lem:delta-bound}, and $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps, q, m, d)$ in the displayed function of Corollary~\ref{cor:pauli-binary}, whose own item~1 reverts to $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps, m, d, q)$; the formula is the same throughout, and here the order $(\eps, m, d, q)$ is used everywhere. Note also two deliberate asymmetries with the classical soundness function of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}: there the polynomial prefactor is $a(dmk)^a$ and the exponent satisfies $0 < b \le 1$, while in Theorems~\ref{thm:pauli} and Corollary~\ref{cor:pauli-binary} the prefactor is $a(md)^a$ and the exponent satisfies the strict inequality $0 < b < 1$.

   108	\section{The source assertion and the obstruction}
   109	
   110	We examine the final step of the subsection ``Applying the classical
   111	low-degree test'' in the analysis of the Pauli basis test in the compression
   112	paper of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen (MIP$^{*}$=RE,
   113	arXiv:2001.04383), whose quantum soundness component builds on the low
   114	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.%
   115	\footnote{Tracked in \localissue{0002}.  In the mirror of the source
   116	consulted here, the polynomial-pair lemma and its proof are at
   117	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
   118	lines~1267--1288; the sub-line lemma is at lines~1063--1116 and the combined
   119	line lemma at lines~1020--1034 of the same file.  The game parametrization
   120	with its divisibility, the index function, the soundness statement with its
   121	proof, and admissibility are at
   122	\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
   123	lines~33--35, 214--219, 413--458, and 958--961.}
   124	There, the combined point measurements
   125	$\{\hat Q^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_c\}$ and combined line measurements
   126	$\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, indexed by points of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and lines in
   127	$\F_q^{2m+2}$, are asserted to form a strategy for the classical low
   128	individual degree game with parameters
   129	\[
   130	  \mathsf{ldparams} = (q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)
   131	  \tag{\path{lem:qld-4-7}}
   132	\]
   133	of value $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$, and the quantum soundness theorem
   134	for that game is applied to produce the global polynomial-pair measurement.
   135	The two lemmas feeding this step are stated for the line-point distribution
   136	over $\F_q^{2m+2}$.
   137	
   138	The game, however, is parametrized by tuples $(q,m',d,k)$ with $q$ an
   139	admissible field size \emph{and $m'$ dividing $q$}.  The divisibility is not
   140	incidental: the question distribution is a conditionally linear distribution
   141	in which a uniform seed coordinate $s \in \F_q$, read as an integer in
   142	$\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, determines the axis or diagonal index through the unique
   143	$\chi(s)$ with
   144	\[
   145	  s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m'} + r, \qquad 0 \le r < \frac{q}{m'},
   146	  \tag{\path{eq:chi-func}}
   147	\]

   149	size $q/m'$ and the index is uniform.  For $m' \nmid q$ neither the index
   150	function nor the line-point distribution built from it is defined.

   153	is a power of two, $m \mid q$ forces $m = 2^j$.  For $j \ge 1$ the integer
   154	$m+1 \ge 3$ is odd, so $2m+2 = 2(m+1)$ has an odd factor exceeding $1$ and

   156	admissible $q$ except $q = 2$.  Thus the instantiation at dimension $2m+2$ is
   157	undefined for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$: for instance

   163	\section{What the cited soundness theorem requires: the import obligations}
   164	\label{sec:import-obligations}
   165	
   166	The quantum soundness theorem for the classical game inherits the constraint
   167	$m' \mid q$ solely because it is stated for the game just described; its
   168	proof fixes an admissible $q$ with $m' \mid q$, asserts that the game with
   169	simultaneity parameter $1$ is \emph{identical} to the two-prover tensor-code
   170	test for the Reed--Solomon tensor code $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$ of the same
   171	authors' \emph{Quantum soundness of testing tensor codes} (arXiv:2111.08131)
   172	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, and concludes by Theorem~4.7 there, instantiated with
   173	that theorem's auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ in that source,
   174	and written $K$ here to avoid clashing with the field exponent and the
   175	simultaneity parameter --- chosen as $(m')^3 d$.  Neither
   176	the asserted identity nor the instantiation is complete as stated, so the
   177	import carries two verification obligations, which this section details and
   178	which the blueprint's proof node for the soundness statement records as
   179	open.  Both obligations are independent of the divisibility question: they
   180	arise at every dimension, for the $\chi$-based game where it is defined and
   181	equally for the directly indexed variant proposed under the candidate
   182	repairs.
   183	
   184	\paragraph{The cited test.}
   185	In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
   186	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
   187	measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
   188	three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
   189	subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
   190	test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
   191	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
   192	direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
   193	send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
   194	$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
   195	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
   196	last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
   197	in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
   198	one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
   199	the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
   200	test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
   201	pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
   202	answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
   203	test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
   204	$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
   205	--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
   206	distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
   207	$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
   208	consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
   209	lines measurements, and with each other, up to
   210	$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
   211	\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.
   212	
   213	\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
   214	The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
   215	is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
   216	(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
   217	two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
   218	--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
   219	question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
   220	polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
   221	diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
   222	and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
   223	both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
   224	description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of
   225	the pair $(u,v)$, so the constructed measurement must average over the
   226	compatible indices and seeds; and the game's diagonal lines fix the
   227	\emph{first} $i-1$ coordinates where the test's subcubes fix the
   228	\emph{last} $j-1$, so the coordinate conventions must be aligned.  The
   229	construction must preserve projectivity and must match the law of the
   230	hidden-subcube pair with the law induced by the game's diagonal sampling.
   231	(ii)~The game's line questions carry the seed $s \in \F_q$; the test's
   232	carry only the line.  A strategy may depend on the seed beyond its class
   233	$\chi^{-1}(i)$, and removing this dependence runs into the fiber-averaging

sed -n '260,520p' docs/mathematical_language.md"","aggregated_output":"# Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |

An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.

File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.

### Shared helpers

When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

## Review Checklist

Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.

- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
      implementation-phase labels)?
- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
      source does not use them that way?
- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
      that order of preference?
- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
      construction they support?
- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the

 The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. +/-- A uniform consistency defect is invariant under a bijective relabeling of
+its question type. -/
+theorem consistencyDefect_uniform_question_equiv
+    {X Y Outcome iota : Type*}
+    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Nonempty X]
+    [Fintype Y] [DecidableEq Y] [Nonempty Y]
+    [Fintype Outcome] [DecidableEq Outcome]
+    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
+    (e : X ≃ Y) (A B : Y → Outcome → Op iota)
+    (psi : EuclideanSpace ℂ iota) :
+    consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution X)
+        (fun x a => A (e x) a) (fun x a => B (e x) a) psi =
+      consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution Y) A B psi := by
+  unfold consistencyDefect
+  simpa using avgOver_uniform_equiv e (fun x =>
+    ∑ a : Outcome, ∑ b : Outcome,
+      if a = b then 0 else
+        (inner ℂ psi ((EuclideanSpace.equiv iota ℂ).symm
+          (((A (e x) a) * (B (e x) b)).mulVec psi))).re)
+
+/-- A consistency defect is invariant under a bijective relabeling of both
+outcome families. -/
+theorem consistencyDefect_outcome_equiv
+    {X Alpha Beta iota : Type*}
+    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X]
+    [Fintype Alpha] [DecidableEq Alpha]
+    [Fintype Beta] [DecidableEq Beta]
+    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
+    (mu : Distribution X) (e : Beta ≃ Alpha)
+    (A B : X → Alpha → Op iota) (psi : EuclideanSpace ℂ iota) :
+    consistencyDefect mu
+        (fun x b => A x (e b)) (fun x b => B x (e b)) psi =
+      consistencyDefect mu A B psi := by
+  unfold consistencyDefect
+  apply avgOver_congr
+  intro x
+  let term : Alpha → Alpha → ℝ := fun a b =>
+    if a = b then 0 else
+      (inner ℂ psi ((EuclideanSpace.equiv iota ℂ).symm
+        (((A x a) * (B x b)).mulVec psi))).re
+  calc
+    _ = ∑ a : Beta, ∑ b : Beta, term (e a) (e b) := by
+      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+      intro a _
+      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+      intro b _
+      unfold term
+      by_cases hab : a = b
+      · subst b
+        simp
+      · have heab : e a ≠ e b := fun h => hab (e.injective h)
+        simp [hab, heab]
+    _ =
+        ∑ a : Beta, ∑ b : Alpha, term (e a) b := by
+      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+      intro a _
+      exact Equiv.sum_comp e (fun b => term (e a) b)
+    _ = ∑ a : Alpha, ∑ b : Alpha, term a b :=
+      Equiv.sum_comp e (fun a => ∑ b : Alpha, term a b)
+    _ = _ := rfl
+
+/-- Simultaneous bijective relabeling of uniform questions and outcomes leaves
+the consistency defect unchanged. -/
+theorem consistencyDefect_uniform_question_outcome_equiv
+    {X Y Alpha Beta iota : Type*}
+    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Nonempty X]
+    [Fintype Y] [DecidableEq Y] [Nonempty Y]
+    [Fintype Alpha] [DecidableEq Alpha]
+    [Fintype Beta] [DecidableEq Beta]
+    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
+    (questionEquiv : X ≃ Y) (outcomeEquiv : Beta ≃ Alpha)
+    (A B : Y → Alpha → Op iota) (psi : EuclideanSpace ℂ iota) :
+    consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution X)
+        (fun x b => A (questionEquiv x) (outcomeEquiv b))
+        (fun x b => B (questionEquiv x) (outcomeEquiv b)) psi =
+      consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution Y) A B psi := by
+  calc
+    consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution X)
+        (fun x b => A (questionEquiv x) (outcomeEquiv b))
+        (fun x b => B (questionEquiv x) (outcomeEquiv b)) psi =
+      consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution X)
+        (fun x a => A (questionEquiv x) a)
+        (fun x a => B (questionEquiv x) a) psi :=
+      consistencyDefect_outcome_equiv (uniformDistribution X)
+        outcomeEquiv _ _ psi
+    _ = consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution Y) A B psi :=
+      consistencyDefect_uniform_question_equiv questionEquiv A B psi

+/-- Pointwise equality of both operator families gives equality of their

+theorem consistencyDefect_congr
+    {X Outcome iota : Type*}
+    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X]
+    [Fintype Outcome] [DecidableEq Outcome]
+    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
+    (mu : Distribution X) (A A' B B' : X → Outcome → Op iota)
+    (psi : EuclideanSpace ℂ iota)
+    (hA : ∀ x a, A x a = A' x a) (hB : ∀ x a, B x a = B' x a) :
+    consistencyDefect mu A B psi = consistencyDefect mu A' B' psi := by
+  unfold consistencyDefect
+  apply avgOver_congr
+  intro x
+  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+  intro a _
+  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+  intro b _
+  by_cases hab : a = b
+  · simp [hab]

+    [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β] [DecidableEq γ]

    29	/-- Parameters for the directly indexed low-degree game.  Unlike `LdParams`,
    30	this directly indexed line-space construction has no divisibility field: its coordinate index is
    31	sampled from `Fin m` rather than encoded by fibers of `chiIndex`.
    32	
    33	This is the direct-index repair described in
    34	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`; it is not a second
    35	definition of the source verifier game. -/
    36	structure DirectLdParams where
    37	  q : ℕ
    38	  m : ℕ
    39	  d : ℕ
    40	  k : ℕ
    41	  hm : 1 ≤ m
    42	  hd : 1 ≤ d
    43	  hk : 1 ≤ k
    44	  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
    45	
    46	/-- The canonical scalar model for directly indexed parameters. -/
    47	noncomputable def DirectLdParams.model (D : DirectLdParams) : FixedFieldModel D.q :=
    48	  fixedFieldModel D.q D.hq
    49	
    50	/-- The scalar field of a directly indexed low-degree game. -/
    51	abbrev DirectScalarQ (D : DirectLdParams) := D.model.K
    52	
    53	/-- The first coordinate, available because directly indexed dimensions are
    54	positive. -/
    55	def DirectLdParams.firstIndex (D : DirectLdParams) : Fin D.m :=
    56	  ⟨0, lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one D.hm⟩
    57	
    58	instance (D : DirectLdParams) : Nonempty (Fin D.m) := ⟨D.firstIndex⟩
    59	
    60	/-- The direct game used at the extended dimension of the combining map.  Its
    61	field, degree, and simultaneity parameters are inherited from `P`, while its
    62	dimension is `2 * P.m + 2`; no divisibility assertion is introduced.
    63	
    64	The construction has dimension `2 * P.m + 2` without requiring
    65	`2 * P.m + 2 ∣ P.q`; it supplies the directly indexed line and coordinate
    66	spaces used in the dimension-extension argument of
    67	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex:1257-1293`.
    68	-/
    69	def AdmissibleParams.extendedDirectLd (P : AdmissibleParams) : DirectLdParams where
    70	  q := P.q
    71	  m := 2 * P.m + 2
    72	  d := P.d
    73	  k := 1
    74	  hm := by omega
    75	  hd := P.hd
    76	  hk := by decide
    77	  hq := P.hq
    78	
    79	/-- A common random sample for the directly indexed question distribution.
    80	The point, coordinate index, and unrestricted direction are mutually uniform. -/
    81	structure DirectLdSpace (D : DirectLdParams) where
    82	  point : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D
    83	  index : Fin D.m
    84	  direction : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D
    85	  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype
    86	
    87	instance (D : DirectLdParams) : Nonempty (DirectLdSpace D) :=
    88	  ⟨⟨0, D.firstIndex, 0⟩⟩
    89	
    90	/-- Decompose a direct sample into its point and the remaining independent
    91	coordinates. -/
    92	private def directLdSpacePointEquiv (D : DirectLdParams) :
    93	    DirectLdSpace D ≃
    94	      (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) ×
    95	        (Fin D.m × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) where
    96	  toFun sample := (sample.point, sample.index, sample.direction)
    97	  invFun sample := ⟨sample.1, sample.2.1, sample.2.2⟩
    98	  left_inv sample := by cases sample; rfl
    99	  right_inv sample := by cases sample; rfl
   100	
   101	/-- Decompose a direct sample into its stored index and the remaining
   102	independent coordinates. -/
   103	def directLdSpaceIndexEquiv (D : DirectLdParams) :
   104	    DirectLdSpace D ≃
   105	      Fin D.m ×
   106	        ((Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) ×
   107	          (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) where
   108	  toFun sample := (sample.index, sample.point, sample.direction)
   109	  invFun sample := ⟨sample.2.1, sample.1, sample.2.2⟩
   110	  left_inv sample := by cases sample; rfl
   111	  right_inv sample := by cases sample; rfl
   112	
   113	/-- Compatibility name for the index-first direct-sample decomposition. -/
   114	abbrev directLdSpaceIndexSplitEquiv (D : DirectLdParams) :
   115	    DirectLdSpace D ≃
   116	      Fin D.m × ((Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :=
   117	  directLdSpaceIndexEquiv D
   118	
   119	/-- Zero the coordinates preceding the directly sampled prefix index. -/
   120	def directPrefixProjection {D : DirectLdParams} (i : Fin D.m)
   121	    (v : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D :=
   122	  fun j => if j.val < i.val then 0 else v j
   123	
   124	/-- Canonical line descriptions whose coordinate index is stored directly.
   125	Coordinates are numbered from zero, so `index = i` represents coordinate
   126	`i + 1` in the paper. -/
   127	inductive DirectLineDesc (D : DirectLdParams) where
   128	  | axis (base : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) (index : Fin D.m)
   129	      (baseFixed : lineRepMap (coordinateDirection index) base = base)
   130	  | diagonal (base : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) (index : Fin D.m)
   131	      (direction : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)
   132	      (baseFixed : lineRepMap direction base = base)
   133	      (prefixZero : ∀ j : Fin D.m, j.val < index.val → direction j = 0)
   134	  deriving DecidableEq
   135	
   136	/-- The kind of a directly indexed line. -/
   137	def DirectLineDesc.kind {D : DirectLdParams} : DirectLineDesc D → LineKind
   138	  | .axis _ _ _ => .axis
   139	  | .diagonal _ _ _ _ _ => .diagonal
   140	
   141	/-- The coordinate index stored in a directly indexed line. -/
   142	def DirectLineDesc.index {D : DirectLdParams} : DirectLineDesc D → Fin D.m
   143	  | .axis _ index _ => index
   144	  | .diagonal _ index _ _ _ => index
   145	
   146	/-- The canonical base point of a directly indexed line. -/
   147	def DirectLineDesc.base {D : DirectLdParams} :
   148	    DirectLineDesc D → Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D
   149	  | .axis base _ _ => base
   150	  | .diagonal base _ _ _ _ => base
   151	
   152	/-- The geometric direction of a directly indexed line. -/
   153	def DirectLineDesc.direction {D : DirectLdParams} (line : DirectLineDesc D) :
   154	    Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D :=
   155	  match line with
   156	  | .axis _ index _ => coordinateDirection index
   157	  | .diagonal _ _ direction _ _ => direction
   158	
   159	/-- The base of a directly indexed description is fixed by its geometric
   160	direction. -/
   161	theorem DirectLineDesc.base_fixed {D : DirectLdParams} (line : DirectLineDesc D) :
   162	    lineRepMap line.direction line.base = line.base := by
   163	  cases line with
   164	  | axis base index baseFixed => exact baseFixed
   165	  | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero => exact baseFixed
   166	
   167	/-- Every directly indexed diagonal description retains its prefix-zero
   168	invariant. -/
   169	theorem DirectLineDesc.diagonal_prefix_zero {D : DirectLdParams}
   170	    (line : DirectLineDesc D) (hline : line.kind = .diagonal) :
   171	    ∀ j : Fin D.m, j.val < line.index.val → line.direction j = 0 := by
   172	  cases line with
   173	  | axis base index baseFixed => simp [DirectLineDesc.kind] at hline
   174	  | diagonal base index direction baseFixed prefixZero => exact prefixZero
   175	
   176	/-- The point set represented by a directly indexed line. -/
   177	noncomputable def DirectLineDesc.pointSet {D : DirectLdParams}
   178	    (line : DirectLineDesc D) : Set (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) :=
   179	  linePoints line.base line.direction
   180	
   181	/-- Turn a direct sample into its canonical axis-line description. -/
   182	noncomputable def directALineDescOf (D : DirectLdParams)
   183	    (sample : DirectLdSpace D) : DirectLineDesc D :=
   184	  let direction := coordinateDirection sample.index
   185	  let base := lineRepMap direction sample.point
   186	  .axis base sample.index (lineRepMap_apply_self direction sample.point)
   187	
   188	/-- Turn a direct sample into its canonical diagonal-line description. -/
   189	noncomputable def directDLineDescOf (D : DirectLdParams)
   190	    (sample : DirectLdSpace D) : DirectLineDesc D :=
   191	  let direction := directPrefixProjection sample.index sample.direction
   192	  let base := lineRepMap direction sample.point
   193	  .diagonal base sample.index direction
   194	    (lineRepMap_apply_self direction sample.point) (by
   195	      intro j hj
   196	      change directPrefixProjection sample.index sample.direction j = 0
   197	      rw [directPrefixProjection, if_pos hj])
   198	
   199	/-- The axis-line/point law with a directly sampled coordinate index. -/
   200	noncomputable def directALinePointDist (D : DirectLdParams) :
   201	    Distribution (DirectLineDesc D × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :=
   202	  (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D)).map fun sample =>
   203	    (directALineDescOf D sample, sample.point)
   204	
   205	/-- The diagonal-line/point law with a directly sampled prefix index. -/
   206	noncomputable def directDLinePointDist (D : DirectLdParams) :
   207	    Distribution (DirectLineDesc D × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :=
   208	  (uniformDistribution (DirectLdSpace D)).map fun sample =>
   209	    (directDLineDescOf D sample, sample.point)
   210	
   211	/-- The equal mixture of the directly indexed axis and diagonal line-point
   212	laws.  This is the replacement for the otherwise undefined extended-dimension
   213	instance used at paper
   214	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1020-1116`. -/
   215	noncomputable def directLinePointDist (D : DirectLdParams) :
   216	    Distribution (DirectLineDesc D × (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)) :=
   217	  Distribution.mix (1 / 2) (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
   218	    (directALinePointDist D) (directDLinePointDist D)
   219	
   220	/-- The directly indexed axis-line/point law is probabilistic. -/
   221	theorem directALinePointDist_isProbability (D : DirectLdParams) :
   222	    (directALinePointDist D).IsProbability := by
   223	  exact (uniformDistribution_isProbability (DirectLdSpace D)).map _
   224	
   225	/-- The directly indexed diagonal-line/point law is probabilistic. -/
   226	theorem directDLinePointDist_isProbability (D : DirectLdParams) :
   227	    (directDLinePointDist D).IsProbability := by
   228	  exact (uniformDistribution_isProbability (DirectLdSpace D)).map _
   229	
   230	/-- The directly indexed line-point mixture is probabilistic. -/
   231	theorem directLinePointDist_isProbability (D : DirectLdParams) :
   232	    (directLinePointDist D).IsProbability := by
   233	  exact Distribution.mix_isProbability _ _ _
   234	    (directALinePointDist_isProbability D) (directDLinePointDist_isProbability D)
   235	    (by norm_num) (by norm_num)

    34	/-- Regard a matrix-valued projective measurement as a projective measurement

    36	noncomputable def matrixMeasurementToLDTProjMeas
    37	    {alpha iota : Type*} [Fintype alpha] [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]

   367	/-- Correlated residue registers turn two block-diagonal effects into the
   368	uniform average of their matching source-block Born weights. -/
   369	private theorem seedFiberBlockBornAmplitude
   370	    {G : Game} (S : Strategy G) (L : LdParams)
   371	    (A : Fin (L.q / L.m) → Op S.ιA)
   372	    (B : Fin (L.q / L.m) → Op S.ιB) :
   373	    vectorBornAmplitude (seedFiberLiftedState S L)
   374	        (Matrix.blockDiagonal A) (Matrix.blockDiagonal B) =
   375	      (Fintype.card (Fin (L.q / L.m)) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
   376	        ∑ residue, vectorBornAmplitude S.ψ (A residue) (B residue) := by
   377	  classical
   378	  letI : Nonempty (Fin (L.q / L.m)) :=
   379	    Fin.pos_iff_nonempty.mp L.seedFiberCard_pos
   380	  unfold vectorBornAmplitude applyOperatorToState heteroKron Matrix.kronecker
   381	  simp_rw [EuclideanSpace.inner_eq_star_dotProduct]

   384	  simp_rw [← Finset.univ_product_univ, Finset.sum_product]

   389	  ring_nf

   391	  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
   392	  rw [← mul_assoc]
   393	  congr 1

     8	/-!
     9	# The directly indexed low-degree game
    10	
    11	The low-degree game used by the Pauli-basis combining argument is needed in
    12	dimension `2 * m + 2`.  The existing conditionally linear game represents a
    13	coordinate index by an equally sized fiber in the scalar field and therefore
    14	requires the dimension to divide the field size.  This file gives the separate
    15	directly indexed variant which samples that index directly.
    16	
    17	The geometric line carrier records the sampled coordinate, and line evaluation
    18	uses an `Option` outcome rather than assigning a value when a point does not
    19	determine one.  The game retains the point, axis-line, and diagonal-line answer
    20	formats and the nine ordered type branches of the original low-degree game.
    21	
    22	The `Transport` modules relate the direct game to the seed-indexed game and to
    23	the low individual degree test: `Transport.Correspondence`
    24	identifies coordinates, answers, and the question law of the two QPBT
    25	presentations; `Transport.SeedFiber` dilates a seed-indexed strategy to a
    26	direct strategy by a correlated residue register, and `Transport.SeedFiberValue`
    27	shows that the dilation preserves the value exactly; `Transport.Questions`
    28	reads LDT lines as canonical direct questions and rebases direct answers;
    29	`Transport.Strategy` reads one coordinate of a projective direct strategy as a
    30	LDT projective strategy, with exact Born-weight formulas for both constructions;
    31	`Transport.Consistency` reexpresses the three single-polynomial LDT consistency
    32	relations in direct coordinates, the first two at a fixed tuple coordinate; and
    33	`Transport.BranchComparison`, `Transport.DiagonalRecursion`, and
    34	`Transport.PassConversion` convert a value bound of the direct game into the
    35	pass hypothesis of the low individual degree theorem for every
    36	coordinate strategy.  `GameValue` supplies the rejection calculus relating the
    37	direct value to the LDT branch weights.
    38

    60	
    61	Throughout, $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size, the tuple
    62	$(q,m,d)$ is admissible when moreover $d \ge 1$ and $m \mid q$, and
    63	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ denotes the $m$-variate polynomial representatives
    64	over $\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$.  The comparison involves four
    65	theorem forms.
    66	\begin{enumerate}
    67	  \item \textbf{Source theorem form} (the polynomial-pair measurement).  There
    68	  is a function $\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$,
    69	  for universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, such that for every
    70	  admissible $(q,m,d)$ and every projective strategy for the Pauli basis test
    71	  succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, there is a projective
    72	  measurement $\{\hat S_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ with outcomes pairs of polynomials in
    73	  $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ whose evaluations are $\delta_S$-consistent, on
    74	  average over a uniform point $u \in \F_q^m$ and in both bases
    75	  $W \in \{X,Z\}$, with the corresponding points measurements
    76	  $\{\hat M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\}$ of the strategy, together with the
    77	  symmetric counterpart of this relation.
    78	  \item \textbf{Missing instantiation obligation.}  The classical low
    79	  individual degree game with parameter tuple $(q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)$ is well
    80	  defined, and the combined point and line measurements assembled in the
    81	  analysis constitute a strategy for it of value at least
    82	  $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$.  The game's question distribution draws
    83	  its axis and diagonal indices through an index function
    84	  $\chi_{2m+2}\colon \F_q \to \{1,\ldots,2m+2\}$ with classes of equal size
    85	  $q/(2m+2)$, so the game exists only when $2m+2$ divides $q$.
    86	  \item \textbf{Restricted form supported by the present route.}  The source
    87	  theorem form under the additional hypothesis $2m+2 \mid q$.  Among
    88	  admissible tuples this hypothesis holds exactly when $m = 1$ and
    89	  $q \ge 8$; it fails for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ and for
    90	  $(q,m) = (2,1)$.
    91	  \item \textbf{Repaired import form} (recommended target).  Quantum
    92	  soundness of the directly indexed variant of the classical low individual
    93	  degree game over $\F_q^{m'}$, for every dimension $m' \ge 1$ and
    94	  admissible $q$, with no divisibility hypothesis: the question
    95	  distribution samples the axis index, and the diagonal prefix index,
    96	  uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly rather than through an index
    97	  function on $\F_q$, and line questions carry the sampled index itself in
    98	  place of the seed $s \in \F_q$; the error is
    99	  $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}(\eps,q,m',d,k) = a(dm'k)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} +
   100	  2^{-bm'd})$.  This is a candidate target form, not an established one:
   101	  proving it carries the same two import obligations as the $\chi$-based
   102	  import (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}), and deriving the present
   103	  form from it when $m' \mid q$ requires the strategy transport described
   104	  under the candidate repairs below, whose synchronicity step is an open
   105	  obligation.

   108	\section{The source assertion and the obstruction}
   109	
   110	We examine the final step of the subsection ``Applying the classical
   111	low-degree test'' in the analysis of the Pauli basis test in the compression
   112	paper of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen (MIP$^{*}$=RE,
   113	arXiv:2001.04383), whose quantum soundness component builds on the low
   114	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.%
   115	\footnote{Tracked in \localissue{0002}.  In the mirror of the source
   116	consulted here, the polynomial-pair lemma and its proof are at
   117	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
   118	lines~1267--1288; the sub-line lemma is at lines~1063--1116 and the combined
   119	line lemma at lines~1020--1034 of the same file.  The game parametrization
   120	with its divisibility, the index function, the soundness statement with its
   121	proof, and admissibility are at
   122	\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
   123	lines~33--35, 214--219, 413--458, and 958--961.}
   124	There, the combined point measurements
   125	$\{\hat Q^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_c\}$ and combined line measurements
   126	$\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, indexed by points of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and lines in
   127	$\F_q^{2m+2}$, are asserted to form a strategy for the classical low
   128	individual degree game with parameters
   129	\[
   130	  \mathsf{ldparams} = (q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)
   131	  \tag{\path{lem:qld-4-7}}
   132	\]
   133	of value $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$, and the quantum soundness theorem
   134	for that game is applied to produce the global polynomial-pair measurement.
   135	The two lemmas feeding this step are stated for the line-point distribution
   136	over $\F_q^{2m+2}$.
   137	
   138	The game, however, is parametrized by tuples $(q,m',d,k)$ with $q$ an
   139	admissible field size \emph{and $m'$ dividing $q$}.  The divisibility is not
   140	incidental: the question distribution is a conditionally linear distribution
   141	in which a uniform seed coordinate $s \in \F_q$, read as an integer in
   142	$\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, determines the axis or diagonal index through the unique
   143	$\chi(s)$ with
   144	\[
   145	  s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m'} + r, \qquad 0 \le r < \frac{q}{m'},
   146	  \tag{\path{eq:chi-func}}
   147	\]
   148	so that the $m'$ classes $\chi^{-1}(i)$ partition $\F_q$ into sets of equal
   149	size $q/m'$ and the index is uniform.  For $m' \nmid q$ neither the index
   150	function nor the line-point distribution built from it is defined.
   151	
   152	Admissibility of $(q,m,d)$ supplies only $m \mid q$.  Since an admissible $q$
   153	is a power of two, $m \mid q$ forces $m = 2^j$.  For $j \ge 1$ the integer
   154	$m+1 \ge 3$ is odd, so $2m+2 = 2(m+1)$ has an odd factor exceeding $1$ and
   155	divides no power of two; for $m = 1$ the condition $4 \mid q$ holds for every
   156	admissible $q$ except $q = 2$.  Thus the instantiation at dimension $2m+2$ is
   157	undefined for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$: for instance
   158	$(q,m,d) = (8,2,1)$ is admissible, while $6 \nmid 8$.  The source performs
   159	the instantiation without addressing the divisibility, so its proof route
   160	establishes the polynomial-pair lemma, and with it the soundness theorem for
   161	the Pauli basis test that rests on it, only for $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.

   163	\section{What the cited soundness theorem requires: the import obligations}
   164	\label{sec:import-obligations}
   165	
   166	The quantum soundness theorem for the classical game inherits the constraint
   167	$m' \mid q$ solely because it is stated for the game just described; its
   168	proof fixes an admissible $q$ with $m' \mid q$, asserts that the game with
   169	simultaneity parameter $1$ is \emph{identical} to the two-prover tensor-code
   170	test for the Reed--Solomon tensor code $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$ of the same
   171	authors' \emph{Quantum soundness of testing tensor codes} (arXiv:2111.08131)
   172	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, and concludes by Theorem~4.7 there, instantiated with
   173	that theorem's auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ in that source,
   174	and written $K$ here to avoid clashing with the field exponent and the
   175	simultaneity parameter --- chosen as $(m')^3 d$.  Neither
   176	the asserted identity nor the instantiation is complete as stated, so the
   177	import carries two verification obligations, which this section details and
   178	which the blueprint's proof node for the soundness statement records as
   179	open.  Both obligations are independent of the divisibility question: they
   180	arise at every dimension, for the $\chi$-based game where it is defined and
   181	equally for the directly indexed variant proposed under the candidate
   182	repairs.
   183	
   184	\paragraph{The cited test.}
   185	In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
   186	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
   187	measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
   188	three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
   189	subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
   190	test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
   191	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
   192	direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
   193	send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
   194	$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
   195	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
   196	last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
   197	in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
   198	one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
   199	the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
   200	test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
   201	pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
   202	answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
   203	test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
   204	$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
   205	--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
   206	distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
   207	$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
   208	consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
   209	lines measurements, and with each other, up to
   210	$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
   211	\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.
   212	
   213	\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
   214	The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
   215	is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
   216	(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
   217	two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
   218	--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
   219	question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
   220	polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
   221	diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
   222	and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
   223	both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
   224	description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of
   225	the pair $(u,v)$, so the constructed measurement must average over the
   226	compatible indices and seeds; and the game's diagonal lines fix the
   227	\emph{first} $i-1$ coordinates where the test's subcubes fix the
   228	\emph{last} $j-1$, so the coordinate conventions must be aligned.  The

   231	(ii)~The game's line questions carry the seed $s \in \F_q$; the test's

   236	(iii)~The branch weights differ: each nontrivial cross-test has mass $1/3$

    10	## References
    11	
    12	The underlying game is `def:ld-game` in
    13	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, with source origin

    26	
    27	/-- Coefficient lists for a univariate polynomial of degree at most `c` in the
    28	direct scalar field. -/
    29	abbrev DirectDegPoly (D : DirectLdParams) (c : ℕ) :=
    30	  Fin (c + 1) → DirectScalarQ D
    31	
    32	/-- A direct line polynomial evaluates to `a` at `u` when `u` lies on the line
    33	and every parameter presenting `u` gives value `a`.  The universal clause
    34	keeps the zero-direction case explicit. -/
    35	def DirectEvaluatesTo {D : DirectLdParams} {c : ℕ} (line : DirectLineDesc D)
    36	    (f : DirectDegPoly D c) (u : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)
    37	    (a : DirectScalarQ D) : Prop :=
    38	  (∃ t : DirectScalarQ D, u = line.base + t • line.direction) ∧
    39	    ∀ t : DirectScalarQ D, u = line.base + t • line.direction →
    40	      evalCoefficient f t = a
    41	
    42	/-- Option-completed evaluation of a direct line polynomial.  `none` is an
    43	explicit outcome when the point does not determine an evaluation; no field
    44	value is used as a fallback. -/
    45	noncomputable def directEvalOpt {D : DirectLdParams} {c : ℕ}
    46	    (line : DirectLineDesc D) (u : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D)
    47	    (f : DirectDegPoly D c) : Option (DirectScalarQ D) := by
    48	  classical
    49	  exact if h : ∃ a : DirectScalarQ D, DirectEvaluatesTo line f u a then
    50	    some (Classical.choose h)
    51	  else none

    53	/-- The typed question alphabet of the directly indexed game. -/
    54	abbrev DirectLdQuestion (D : DirectLdParams) := LdType × DirectLdSpace D
    55	
    56	/-- Canonicalize a common direct sample for one question type.  Irrelevant
    57	coordinates are fixed, so point questions reveal no sampled line index and
    58	axis-line questions reveal no diagonal direction. -/
    59	noncomputable def directLdMap (D : DirectLdParams) :
    60	    LdType → DirectLdSpace D → DirectLdSpace D
    61	  | .point, sample => ⟨sample.point, D.firstIndex, 0⟩
    62	  | .aline, sample =>
    63	      let direction := coordinateDirection sample.index
    64	      ⟨lineRepMap direction sample.point, sample.index, 0⟩
    65	  | .dline, sample =>
    66	      let direction := directPrefixProjection sample.index sample.direction
    67	      ⟨lineRepMap direction sample.point, sample.index, direction⟩
    68	
    69	/-- The directly indexed question distribution.  It has the same uniform
    70	ordered type-pair branches as `ldQuestionDistribution`, but its common sample
    71	contains an actual coordinate index rather than a field seed. -/
    72	noncomputable def directLdQuestionDistribution (D : DirectLdParams) :
    73	    Distribution (DirectLdQuestion D × DirectLdQuestion D) :=
    74	  (uniformDistribution ((LdType × LdType) × DirectLdSpace D)).map fun sample =>
    75	    ((sample.1.1, directLdMap D sample.1.1 sample.2),
    76	      (sample.1.2, directLdMap D sample.1.2 sample.2))

    78	/-- The directly indexed question law is probabilistic. -/
    79	theorem directLdQuestionDistribution_isProbability (D : DirectLdParams) :
    80	    (directLdQuestionDistribution D).IsProbability := by
    81	  exact (uniformDistribution_isProbability
    82	    ((LdType × LdType) × DirectLdSpace D)).map _

    84	/-- The answer alphabet of the directly indexed game. -/
    85	inductive DirectLdAnswer (D : DirectLdParams) where
    86	  | pointVals (a : Fin D.k → DirectScalarQ D)
    87	  | alinePolys (a : Fin D.k → Fin (D.d + 1) → DirectScalarQ D)
    88	  | dlinePolys (a : Fin D.k → Fin (D.m * D.d + 1) → DirectScalarQ D)

    91	/-- A finite code for the directly indexed answer alphabet. -/
    92	abbrev DirectLdAnswerCode (D : DirectLdParams) :=
    93	  (Fin D.k → DirectScalarQ D) ⊕
    94	    ((Fin D.k → Fin (D.d + 1) → DirectScalarQ D) ⊕
    95	      (Fin D.k → Fin (D.m * D.d + 1) → DirectScalarQ D))

    97	/-- Constructor-preserving equivalence between the inductive answer type and
    98	its finite code. -/
    99	noncomputable def directLdAnswerEquiv (D : DirectLdParams) :
   100	    DirectLdAnswer D ≃ DirectLdAnswerCode D where
   101	  toFun
   102	    | .pointVals a => .inl a
   103	    | .alinePolys a => .inr (.inl a)
   104	    | .dlinePolys a => .inr (.inr a)
   105	  invFun
   106	    | .inl a => .pointVals a
   107	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePolys a
   108	    | .inr (.inr a) => .dlinePolys a
   109	  left_inv := by intro answer; cases answer <;> rfl
   110	  right_inv := by
   111	    intro answer
   112	    rcases answer with a | a
   113	    · rfl
   114	    · rcases a with a | a <;> rfl

   120	  Fintype.ofEquiv (DirectLdAnswerCode D) (directLdAnswerEquiv D).symm

   122	/-- Check that a direct-game answer has the constructor required by its
   123	question type. -/

   127	  | .point, .pointVals _ => true
   128	  | .aline, .alinePolys _ => true
   129	  | .dline, .dlinePolys _ => true
   130	  | _, _ => false

   132	/-- The directly indexed axis-line versus point acceptance relation. -/
   133	def directAlinePointCondition (D : DirectLdParams)
   134	    (line point : DirectLdSpace D)
   135	    (f : Fin D.k → Fin (D.d + 1) → DirectScalarQ D)
   136	    (a : Fin D.k → DirectScalarQ D) : Prop :=

   142	def directDlinePointCondition (D : DirectLdParams)
   143	    (line point : DirectLdSpace D)
   144	    (f : Fin D.k → Fin (D.m * D.d + 1) → DirectScalarQ D)
   145	    (a : Fin D.k → DirectScalarQ D) : Prop :=
